translations.blog.5-common-problems-installing-a-natu:
1. Filtration that does not match the pool

The swimming area is only part of the design. Water volume, use, surrounding vegetation and the chosen filtration system also matter. A filter zone copied from another garden is not a sizing calculation for yours.

Ask the designer to show the swimming area, filtration and equipment on the same plan, and explain how the system suits your intended use. Our guide to biological filtration explains the different jobs involved.

2. Leaves and surface water entering the pool

Look at the site after rain as well as on a sunny day. Where does water run from lawns, paths and beds? Where do leaves collect? These observations help the designer plan edges, drainage and access for removing debris.

Sun and shade also affect how you use the garden and which plants suit it. There is no single orientation that resolves every site: assess the surroundings and the proposed system together.

3. Ground and sealing that have not been assessed

The base, changes in level, groundwater and existing structures need attention before excavation. The waterproof lining must suit the design, with careful treatment of edges and any penetrations. An attractive finish cannot compensate for an unsuitable foundation.

Ask what the initial assessment covers and which ground conditions could change the scope or quotation. Make access for machinery and the handling of excavated soil part of that conversation.

4. Circulation treated as an afterthought

The pump, pipework, collection points and return flow work together. Their locations also determine whether equipment is reachable for servicing. Ask to see the water's route through the proposed pool, rather than choosing a pump by its headline capacity alone.

If you already have green or cloudy water, start with the algae troubleshooting guide and record the symptoms before deciding whether equipment needs changing.

5. Planting and care left until the end

Choose plants for the system, planting depths and local conditions. Include room to reach them and remove cut material. A nature pool still needs care, even though it uses biological treatment.

Before handover, agree which checks you will make, how the equipment is maintained and what the seasonal plan involves. The aim is a pool you can live with, not just a completed construction.

What to bring to the first conversation

  • Photos of the garden and access from the road.
  • Your preferred swimming area and how you want to use it.
  • Known ground, drainage or existing-pool issues.
  • Your budget and the care you are willing to take on.

Compare pool options and starting prices to find a useful starting point for that conversation.
Start with the appearance of the problem

Algae attached to stones or plants are different from green water throughout the pond. Aquascape™'s guide to identifying algae distinguishes string algae from suspended algae. Identifying the appearance is a starting point, not a complete diagnosis.

Take photographs from the same spot and note when the change began. Is it concentrated near a waterfall, on the bottom or across the water? Has the colour or smell changed suddenly?

Look for what has entered the water

Check for leaves, cut grass, soil washed from a bed or recent work beside the pool. In a fish pond, record feeding and changes in the fish population too. A recurring problem after rain calls for a look at the surrounding ground as well as the filter.

Remove accessible loose debris according to the care plan. Avoid making several changes at once: you want to understand what helped and whether the cause remains.

Check collection points and circulation

Compare the current water level and flow with the normal operation shown at handover. Is a collection basket full? Is the return flow different? Has a pump stopped or been switched to a different setting? Follow the equipment instructions before opening or cleaning components.

Mechanical collection and biological treatment have different jobs. Read how nature-pool filtration works before assuming that every part of the system should be cleaned in the same way.

Separate advice for swimming water and fish ponds

A product sold for an ornamental pond is not automatically suitable for a swimming pool. Nor can a fish pond's care routine simply be copied into a bathing installation. Before using an additive or changing treatment, check the intended use, the system instructions and the cause of the problem.

Plant choice and quantity also belong to the individual design. Adding an unfamiliar species or shading the whole surface is not a universal remedy.

When the water needs assessment

Appearance alone cannot establish whether water is suitable for bathing. Follow your monitoring plan and seek an assessment if quality is uncertain, especially after an unexplained change. Keep your observations, recent maintenance and equipment details together so the person assessing the system has something concrete to work from.

Prevent the same problem returning

Use the seasonal care guide to plan debris removal and routine checks, then adapt the schedule to your own installation. Repeated problems need an explanation, not just repeated treatment.

Tell us about your existing water feature and the change you have noticed. If you are planning a new pool, see how we approach its design and care.
translations.blog.build.bodyHtml:
How does a nature pool work?

A nature pool works by mimicking natural processes to keep the water clean and clear. Instead of chlorine and chemical filters, biological filters and special plants are used that are effective in breaking down organic material and purifying the water.

A nature pool consists of two main parts: a swimming zone and a regeneration zone. The swimming zone is where you bathe, while the regeneration zone is where the purification process occurs. Water circulates between these zones using a pump. The regeneration zone is filled with gravel, sand, and aquatic plants such as reeds, irises, and water lilies. These plants act as a natural filter that breaks down dirt and improves water quality. A well-functioning nature pool requires that the regeneration zone is large enough and properly designed to handle the amount of water and organic material introduced.

Benefits of a nature pool

There are many benefits to having a nature pool. Firstly, it is completely chemical-free, making the water much gentler on the skin and overall health. This is especially important for children or individuals with sensitive skin who often have issues with chlorine in traditional pools. Nature pools are also environmentally friendly as they do not require chemical additives or frequent water changes.

Visually, nature pools are something entirely different from regular pools. They can be designed to resemble a natural pond and blend into the landscape in a way that traditional pools never can. Additionally, you can plant beautiful aquatic plants in the regeneration zone, creating an oasis of greenery. Operating costs are also low since the system is self-cleaning once properly installed. The combination of aesthetics, sustainability, and low operating costs makes a nature pool an attractive choice for many.

How to build a nature pool yourself

Building a nature pool yourself requires careful planning and understanding of how the system works. The first step is to choose a suitable location for the pool. A sunny spot is ideal as the sun promotes plant growth and improves the efficiency of the regeneration zone. Next, it's time to plan the design of the pool, including size and shape. The swimming zone and regeneration zone should be well-balanced, and the regeneration zone should be roughly the same size as the swimming zone to ensure optimal purification.

Once the design is complete, excavation work begins. Dig both the swimming zone and the regeneration zone to the correct depth, ensuring the ground is stable. Avoid areas with roots or stones that could cause problems. After excavation is complete, a waterproof membrane is installed to protect the pool from leaks.

The next step is to install biological filters and water pumps that keep the water circulating between the zones. It is important to choose the right equipment to ensure the system functions properly. After installation, it's time to plant the plants in the regeneration zone. Choose plants known for their purifying properties, such as reeds and irises. Plant them in the right quantity and placement to optimize purification. Finally, fill the pool with water and start the system. Keep in mind that it may take a few weeks for the plants to establish themselves and for the system to function fully.

Common mistakes when building a nature pool

Building a nature pool yourself is a comprehensive project, and it's easy to make mistakes if you lack experience. One of the most common mistakes is making the regeneration zone too small in relation to the swimming zone. If the zone does not have enough plants or gravel, it cannot purify the water properly, leading to cloudiness and imbalance in the system.

Another pitfall is poor drainage around the pool. If the ground is not properly prepared, water from the surroundings can flow into the pool, bringing soil and organic material that disrupts the system. Incorrect choice of plants is also a common cause of problems. If the plants in the regeneration zone are not suitable for the purpose, purification will not work, which may require you to redo the work. Finally, it is important that the membrane used for sealing is of high quality and installed correctly. Even small leaks can cause major problems and lead to costly repairs.

Cost to build a nature pool

Building a nature pool yourself can be cost-effective compared to hiring a professional installer, but it is important to understand the costs. Material costs for a smaller nature pool can start at around 50,000–100,000 kronor excluding VAT, but this depends on size, material choice, and what components you need to purchase. However, if you make mistakes that require repairs or rework, the costs can quickly exceed the budget.

Is it better to hire a professional?

While it is possible to build a nature pool yourself, it is not without risks. A single mistake, such as incorrectly sized regeneration zone or poor sealing, can lead to problems that are both time-consuming and expensive to fix. Professional installers have the experience and knowledge to eliminate these risks and create a sustainable and well-functioning nature pool from the start.

By hiring an expert, you can get help with everything from design and ground preparation to installation and choosing the right plants. The result is a pool that works just as it should and requires minimal maintenance. If you want to ensure that your nature pool becomes an investment that lasts for many years, it is a good idea to consider getting help from a professional. It can save both time, money, and worries in the long run.

At Faunapoolen, we are happy to help you realize your dream of a nature pool. We offer a free phone consultation where we go through your needs and concerns together.
translations.blog.can-i-use-water-storage-solutions-w:
Collecting rainwater can supplement garden watering when a well is not available. It does not create a continuous supply: the result depends on rainfall, the collecting surface, storage and demand. Begin with the intended use, then calculate whether the water available is useful for that purpose.

What will the collected water be used for?

Watering planting, replenishing a decorative feature and supplying a swimming system are different uses. Record them separately, including when each needs water. The quality requirements and equipment must match the use. Water collected from a roof should not be assumed to be drinking water or ready for bathing.

For a pond or other feature, start with the kind of garden water landscape you are planning. Its water needs belong in the same discussion as the collection system.

How much can the roof and storage provide?

One millimetre of rain over one square metre corresponds to one litre before losses. For example, 10 millimetres on a 100-square-metre roof gives a theoretical 1,000 litres. This is an illustrative calculation, not a prediction of the amount reaching a tank: collection losses, filtering, overflow and existing tank contents affect what can be stored.

Compare local rainfall patterns with the periods when you need water. Annual rainfall alone does not show whether a tank will contain enough during a dry spell. Estimate demand over that period and examine both a small and a larger storage option before choosing a size.

Plan cleaning, filtration and access

Draw the route from the roof through collection and filtering to storage and intended use. Consider how leaves and sediment are removed, how equipment is reached and where overflow goes. Cleaning should remain possible after paving and planting are in place.

Aquascape™ describes modular storage in its rainwater collection products, including AquaBlox used within a lined reservoir. The modules provide storage structure; the full installation still needs a design for its site and use. This product example does not establish what is included in a Faunapoolen quotation.

Assess suitability before using it in a nature pool

Discuss the proposed water source with the person responsible for the pool's design and water-quality plan. What reaches the roof and storage can affect the water collected. A general biological cleaning system does not by itself establish that every source is suitable for swimming.

Allow for drought and check current local conditions

When no rain arrives, a store can run out. Plan which uses take priority and what happens when the level is low. Before agreeing the installation or a filling plan, check current requirements with the relevant water provider and municipality. Any connection to another water supply needs appropriate professional assessment.

Plan storage together with the garden

Location affects excavation, access, the route to planting and future servicing. The garden-planning guide helps you consider those relationships before the visible surfaces are finished.

Have a roof sketch, photographs, intended uses and an estimate of demand ready. Describe your garden and water-storage question in the enquiry notes, so we can discuss the scope and whether we can help with your project.
translations.blog.creating-harmony-intergrating-water:
A nature pool, pond or waterfall works best in a garden when its position supports the way you want to use the place. Begin with where you sit, walk and look out from the house. Then plan the water together with its surroundings, including the space needed for care.

Start with the places where you want to spend time

Mark the breakfast spot, the terrace and a quieter corner on a simple plan. Note which views matter from indoors and where you would enjoy hearing moving water. A waterfall near a seat becomes part of that experience; farther away, its visual connection may matter more.

Try viewing the proposed location at different times of day. Record shade, wind exposure and nearby trees as observations for the design conversation, rather than choosing a location from a single photograph.

Place swimming, seating and paths together

For a nature pool, sketch the route from changing to entering the water and the space for sitting afterwards. Leave room to pass someone at the edge and to reach equipment without crossing a crowded seating area. A larger swimming area is useful only if the whole arrangement still works.

The guide to how much space a nature pool needs explains why the advertised swimming area is only one part of the footprint.

Use changes in level with care

A slope can suggest a stream or waterfall, but also raises questions about access, ground support and where surface water goes. Ask for those questions to be assessed before fixing the shape. Make collection points and equipment reachable without dismantling the landscape around them.

Choose materials that connect the garden

Look at the existing house, terrace and paths before adding a new material. Repeating a stone tone or an edge detail can help the water feel at home. Discuss how the surface feels underfoot, how it meets the water and how it will be maintained, as well as how it looks when newly installed.

Plan plants, views and lighting together

Consider mature plant size so that a clear view today does not become blocked later. Keep the access points and maintenance routes readable. Lighting can help people see the route and changes in level; its position should also consider glare from the water and the view from neighbouring properties.

Our nature-pool project on southern Gotland offers a real example of water within a garden. Use the images to discuss details you like, while planning the arrangement around your own site.

When a pond, stream or fountain fits better

If you mainly want moving water beside a seat, a fountain or waterfall may answer the wish without a bathing area. A planted pond creates a different focal point; a koi pond also brings fish-care requirements that must shape the design. These are different uses with different maintenance needs.

Explore our garden water features and the article on water in a small garden for those options.

Turn inspiration into a proposal for your site

Bring a simple plan, photographs and a short list of the moments you want the garden to make possible. Distinguish your essentials from details that can change. If swimming is the priority, compare nature-pool options for your garden as a starting point for the conversation.
translations.blog.difference.bodyHtml:
What is a natural pool?

A natural pool, also called a biological pool or ecological pool, is an environmentally friendly alternative to a traditional chlorine pool. Instead of chemicals, natural purification methods are used where plants and microorganisms keep the water clean. It creates a pool without chemicals where you can swim without chlorine and enjoy a natural bathing place at home.

Advantages of a natural pool:

  • No chemicals – The water is biologically purified, making the bathing experience gentler for both people and the environment.
  • Healthier water – Perfect for sensitive skin and allergy sufferers who want to avoid chlorine.
  • Lower operating costs – No expensive chemical handling or energy-intensive filtration.
  • Naturally aesthetic – A natural pool blends into the garden and creates a beautiful, harmonious environment.
  • Sustainable choice – A sustainable pool that benefits both the ecosystem and your economy in the long run.
  • Less maintenance – Maintaining a natural pool requires fewer efforts than a traditional pool.

How does a nature pool work?

Instead of using chlorine to purify the water, a natural pool operates through biological filtration. Water flows through plant zones where specific plants and microorganisms break down dirt and nutrients. This means you can enjoy a pool without chemicals, just like in a natural lake.

Difference between a natural pool and a regular pool

The biggest difference between a natural pool and a traditional pool is the purification method. A regular pool requires regular additions of chlorine and chemicals to keep the water sterile, while a natural pool is based on a natural ecosystem. Both options have their pros and cons depending on your priorities.

Advantages of a traditional pool:

  • Quick and effective purification – Chlorine quickly kills bacteria and algae.
  • Temperature control – Easy to heat and use year-round.
  • Standard solution – There are many ready-made pool packages to choose from.

Disadvantages of a traditional pool:

  • Chlorine can cause skin irritation and eye discomfort, especially for sensitive individuals.
  • Higher operating costs as chemicals and advanced filtration are required continuously.
  • Less environmentally friendly as chlorine and other chemicals can negatively impact the ecosystem.

Cost of a natural pool – what should you consider?

Many wonder what the cost of building a natural pool is. Compared to a regular pool, the initial cost may be slightly higher, especially if you want a customized ecosystem and design. However, a natural pool often has lower operating costs since you avoid buying chlorine and other chemicals.

Maintaining a natural pool is also simpler and cheaper in the long run. Since the biological system takes care of itself, you don't need to spend as much time and money on water purification.

Building a natural pool – what should you consider?

If you are considering building a natural pool, it is important to think through both design and function. Natural pools can be designed in many different ways, from modern geometric shapes to more organic and pond-like solutions. Regardless of style, it is important to ensure good water flow and choose the right plants.

Here’s how you can build a natural pool:

  • Plan size and design – Do you want a modern pool or a more natural bathing area at home?
  • Choose the right plants – These act as natural filters and help keep the water clean.
  • Build a stable structure – A well-planned natural pool lasts for many years without major renovation needs.
  • Optimize water flow – The placement of filtration zones and plants plays an important role in water quality.

Is a natural pool the right choice for you?

If you want a pool without chemicals and a more natural bathing experience, a natural pool is an excellent choice. It is gentler on both people and the environment, requires less maintenance, and can save money in the long run. Additionally, it becomes a beautiful part of your garden and creates a sustainable pool where the ecosystem can interact naturally. By adding design elements like stone paving, wooden decks, or stylish lighting, a natural pool can also feel both luxurious and modern.

Regardless of which pool type you choose, it is important to plan carefully and select what best suits your lifestyle and needs. At Faunapoolen, we have expertise in both natural pools and traditional pools, and we are happy to help you find the best solution for you.
translations.blog.din-naturpool-skotsel-efter-install:
Your pool is finished. Here is your new routine

We have finished installing your nature pool. Now it is yours to enjoy: a swim before breakfast, a dip after gardening, an evening beside the water. Keeping it in good condition becomes part of looking after the garden, with a few small habits and some seasonal attention.

Keep this checklist alongside your handover instructions. The timings below are a starting routine; your pool's equipment, planting and surroundings decide how often each task is needed. The operating settings, cleaning methods and water checks agreed for your installation always come first.

What you can leave behind from a chlorine pool

In a conventional swimming pool, disinfectant is used to control microorganisms. In your nature pool, useful microorganisms are part of the cleaning system. Bacteria living on filter surfaces help break down organic matter, while filtration and, where included, plants help manage nutrients. Your job is to keep that system working and remove debris before it builds up.

  • No routine chlorine dosing or shock chlorination. You do not need to buy, store and add chlorine to maintain a disinfectant residual in a pool designed for biological filtration.
  • No chlorine-level adjustment. You still follow the water-testing plan for your pool, including any agreed pH, nutrient or hygiene checks. Natural filtration does not make testing unnecessary.
  • No need to scrub every surface sterile. Protect the living filter while keeping steps and swimming surfaces clean. A natural film on submerged stone is different from a slippery step that needs attention.

The benefit is a different kind of care, without the routine chlorine treatment. It is not a promise of no maintenance, and bacteria do not make leaves or accumulated sediment disappear. Our filtration guide explains what happens along the way.

On days you use the pool

  • Look at the water and the flow. Check that circulation looks as it did at handover and that the water level is within the range you were shown. Investigate a new noise, weak flow or a sudden drop in level.
  • Lift out leaves and other floating debris. Use a net before they sink, especially after wind or heavy leaf fall. Remove what you collect from the pool edge so it cannot wash back in.
  • Check the way into the water. Keep steps and access surfaces clear and clean slippery patches with the method shown for your materials.
  • Rinse off before swimming. Keep soil, grass clippings, soap and garden fertilizer out of the water. Avoid washing tools or rinsing cleaning products into the pool.

Once a week, and after windy weather

  • Check the skimmer basket or debris screen. Empty collected material before it restricts flow. Check more often when leaves are falling; follow the equipment's shutdown and isolation instructions before opening or servicing it.
  • Look for deposits in the swimming area. Remove settled debris with the pool vacuum or compatible cleaning equipment specified for your pool when needed. Keep it out of the planted filter area unless your instructions say otherwise.
  • Check plants and the pool edge. Remove loose dead plant material and keep soil, mulch and lawn cuttings from entering the water. Leave established roots and filter gravel undisturbed during routine care.
  • Check whether water needs topping up. Use the approved water source and filling method, within any local restrictions. Repeated or unexplained water loss needs investigation, not just another refill.
  • Record the checks in your care plan. Complete water tests when scheduled and note unusual readings, changes in appearance or maintenance you have done. A short note helps us advise you if something changes.

Let the living filter do its work

A debris basket catches leaves; a biological filter provides a home for useful microorganisms. They need different care. Emptying the basket does not mean washing out the biological filter every week. Clean or flush that filter only at the interval and in the way specified for your installation.

Keep circulation on its agreed operating schedule. Do not turn it off between swims or change its settings to save electricity without checking with us. Avoid chlorine, disinfectants, household cleaners and off-the-shelf algae treatments. Add bacteria products or other treatments only if they are part of your pool's care plan, with the specified product and dose.

During the first season, the biological system needs time to establish. Ask us about changes rather than trying to correct every trace of algae with a product. Persistent cloudiness, a new smell or a marked change in the water needs assessment; clear-looking water alone does not confirm bathing quality. If contamination is suspected, pause swimming and contact us.

A little extra care when the seasons change

  • Spring: inspect edges and access after frost, remove dead plant material and accumulated sediment as directed, and restart equipment in the prescribed order. Complete the agreed water checks before swimming resumes.
  • Summer: keep up the small tasks, watch water levels in dry weather and check baskets more often after busy swimming days or storms. Arrange for someone to cover the routine while you are away.
  • Autumn: collect leaves more frequently and cut plants back according to the planting plan. If a leaf net is specified, fit and remove it as instructed; it is not a safety cover.
  • Before frost and through winter: follow your pool's winter plan for pumps, pipework, water level and cleaning equipment. Do not improvise a shutdown or drain the pool. Different installations need different frost protection.

For more detail, keep our seasonal care guide with this checklist. Plan any specialist service before you need it, especially ahead of winter.

Prefer to leave the care to us?

You can enjoy your nature pool without taking on all the upkeep yourself. For a small fee, Faunapoolen can help with the care or look after it for you. Whether you need a hand with one task, seasonal care or ongoing help, we agree the work and price with you beforehand.

Email us about care for your pool. Tell us what you would like help with, and we will take it from there.
translations.blog.how-faunapoolen-helps-golf-clubs-ma:
A useful plan for golf-course ponds and streams begins with their function. A visible water feature, an irrigation store and a part of the drainage system may look similar, but they serve different purposes. Record those purposes before choosing maintenance work or new equipment.

Define each pond's role on the course

Give every pond and stream an identifier on the course plan. Note whether it is used for irrigation, receives runoff, has a landscape role or fulfils several functions. Identify who manages it and what information is already available about its construction and operation.

A water level that suits one purpose may conflict with another. Record the desired conditions and known limitations so that an assessment starts with the course's requirements rather than a generic garden-pond solution.

Inventory flows, banks and existing equipment

Mark known inlets, outlets, overflow routes, pumps and pipes. Add accessible records of water levels and changes after rain or irrigation. Note damage at banks, difficult access points and places where debris collects. Photographs taken from the same position make changes easier to compare.

This inventory is a starting point for investigation, not a substitute for a hydrological or engineering assessment. Unknown connections and changes affecting other land need the appropriate expertise.

Track sediment, plants and water quality

Keep observations of sediment, plant growth, odour and water appearance together with maintenance records. If an issue recurs, note the timing, weather and work performed before it appeared. A consistent record is more useful than treating every change as an isolated event.

Our article on algae in ponds explains initial observations. Any treatment must be assessed for the actual water use, connected environments and applicable requirements.

Plan work around the season and play

Coordinate access for equipment with course operations. Agree where removed material can be handled, which areas need protection and how the site is left after work. Give recurring checks a named owner, a schedule suited to the installation and a way to report changes that need attention.

For supplementary storage questions, read the rainwater collection article. A garden-storage example is not a design for course-wide irrigation; demand and supply need their own assessment.

Identify questions that need specialist assessment

Changes to water levels, outlets, excavation or connections to other waters can require specialist investigation and contact with the responsible authority. Establish what applies to the particular site before commissioning that work. Ask prospective suppliers to describe the work they can undertake and any specialists needed.

For projects in Sweden, the Swedish Agency for Marine and Water Management provides guidance on notification of water operations. Use it to prepare questions for the responsible authority; it does not determine the requirements for a particular course.

Prepare for an initial conversation

  • A course plan showing the relevant waters and known connections.
  • Photos, approximate dimensions and existing equipment details.
  • The function of each water body and the issue you want to resolve.
  • Available records, previous work and seasonal access constraints.
  • The person responsible for the decision and ongoing care.

Our water-landscape page shows the kinds of features we discuss. Describe the course's water features in the enquiry notes, including the location and intended work. We can then discuss whether the project fits our scope and what needs assessing first.
translations.blog.how-filtering-works-with-nature-poo:
Follow the water through the system

A useful way to understand a proposal is to follow one complete circuit: water leaves the swimming area, passes through collection and treatment, then returns. The exact arrangement depends on the design. A planted regeneration zone and a constructed wetland filter are not interchangeable simply because both contain plants.

Water route in principle: Swimming area → debris collection → biological treatment → return to the swimming area.

Ask where debris is collected, where the biological filter sits and how the water returns. These three points should be clear on your plan.

Collecting leaves and other debris

Mechanical collection captures material that needs removing from the system. A skimmer or a designed collection area can make leaves easier to reach before they settle elsewhere. Emptying that collection point is part of the owner's routine; collecting debris does not make it disappear.

What the biological filter does

Filter material provides surfaces where microorganisms can develop. Biological processes help break down organic waste, while plants take up nutrients as they grow. This is different from simply straining particles out of the water.

Aquascape™ describes this distinction in its overview of pond filtration. That explanation concerns pond systems; it is not a specification or a bathing-water assessment for an individual swimming pool.

Plants have a role, but are not the whole filter

The planting plan needs to suit the treatment design, water depth and local conditions. A decorative plant at the edge is not a substitute for correctly planned filtration. There is no universal percentage of planting that can be applied to every type of nature pool.

Plant care also needs access. Removing cut stems and leaves is easier when it has been allowed for in the design.

Circulation connects the parts

Pump selection depends on the route the water travels, including pipework, level changes and equipment. The stated maximum pump capacity alone does not describe the flow through a completed installation. Plan servicing access alongside the water route.

Our guide to problems to prevent before building explains why these decisions belong together.

What you still need to check

At handover, establish how to check water level, collection points and circulation, and which cleaning and seasonal tasks apply. Follow the system's monitoring plan: clear-looking water alone does not establish bathing-water quality.

If the appearance changes, use the algae guide to record useful observations before changing equipment or treatment. To plan a new installation, compare our nature-pool options and discuss the site with us.
translations.blog.hur-mycket-plats-behover-en-naturpo:
Start with the swim you want

A quick dip, children playing together and swimming lengths ask different things of a pool. Before choosing a size, describe your ordinary summer evening: how many people are in the water, where you enter, and whether you want a clear swimming route. A long, narrow area and a wider shape can occupy similar areas while feeling very different in use.

Mark your preferred swimming area on a rough garden plan. Keep the terrace, a route from the house and the parts of the garden you still want to use. Walk that route outside. The most useful first question is whether the pool belongs in daily life there, rather than whether a rectangle fits between two boundaries.

Draw the whole installation

Swimming area is not total footprint. A proposal needs to show where treatment happens, where equipment can be reached, how the edge is built and how people move around the water. Their arrangement depends on the selected system and the site; there is no single reliable multiplier from swimming area to required garden area.

  • Water for swimming: usable shape, entry points and the depth agreed for its intended use.
  • Treatment and equipment: the actual filtration design, pipe routes and space to inspect or remove components.
  • Edges and movement: the finished surround, paths, seating and planned protection around the water.
  • Access: room for everyday care and a separate plan for getting machinery and materials onto the site.

Ask for these areas on the same scaled plan before comparing proposals. A photograph cannot tell you how much equipment is hidden outside the frame. Our package comparison is a starting point for swimming area and scope; the complete layout must be assessed for your property.

Leave room to look after it

Imagine lifting a basket, inspecting a connection or removing a pump for service. If those tasks require climbing over planting or moving heavy furniture, the layout needs another look. Ask which parts require access, how often, and what must remain clear. A beautiful edge should still allow the agreed maintenance to happen.

Construction access is a different question. Record the narrowest gate, changes in level, tight turns and any structures above the route. The contractor can then choose a workable method and explain what protection or temporary removal is needed. Agree how disturbed paths and planting will be reinstated, rather than assuming that work is included.

Understand the ground before fixing the shape

Show existing slopes, retaining walls, trees and places where water collects after rain. Tell us about known rock, previous excavation or buried installations. These are questions for assessment, not reasons to guess a standard foundation or drainage solution from a photograph.

Before excavation, establish where services run. Ledningskollen sends enquiries to participating utility owners near the work area. Also identify privately installed pipes and cables; a returned map should not be treated as proof that everything underground has been recorded.

Make a smaller garden work as a garden

Reducing swimming space can be sensible when the priority is a daily dip. Removing necessary treatment or service access is a different compromise. Compare complete layouts, including safety and seating, before deciding that the smallest pool is the best use of the plot.

If movement and the sound of water matter more than swimming, a smaller water feature may suit the garden better. It has a different purpose and still needs an appropriate design and care plan. You can explore those options through our water features.

Prepare a useful first conversation

Bring a simple plan with approximate dimensions, photographs from the house and access route, your location and a short description of how you want to swim. Note what you want to keep and any known ground constraints. Rough information is enough to begin; it is not a substitute for the later site assessment.

Compare the natural pool packages, then tell us which direction appeals to you. If the space is uncertain, you can ask about your garden without choosing a package.

Source checked: 17 September 2026. Final dimensions, construction access and system layout are established for the individual project.
translations.blog.naturpool-10-vanliga-fragor.bodyHtm:
1. How much does a nature pool cost?

The cost of building a nature pool depends mainly on its size, ground conditions, filtration and the work around it. A small natural pool for cooling off is a different project from a larger swimming area with waterfalls and terraces. Our nature pool packages and current starting prices help you compare sizes and what is included.

When comparing natural pool prices, check whether excavation, soil removal, electricity, water filling and garden finishing are included. Rock and difficult access can make a substantial difference. Separate the construction budget from nature pool running costs: circulation, optional heating and regular care need their own allowance.

2. What are the disadvantages of a nature pool?

A nature pool needs space for filtration and regular care. Leaves need removing, and excess nutrients or poor circulation can lead to algae or cloudy water. Plants and small creatures are also part of the setting. Many common nature pool problems can be prevented through careful design and a suitable care routine.

A conventional chlorine pool also needs cleaning and filtration, alongside checks and adjustments to chlorine and pH levels. A nature pool removes the need for routine chlorine dosing and gives you a swimming space that forms part of the garden. Total maintenance depends on the design and equipment in either case, but swimming without chlorine treatment is a clear benefit if that is what you value.

3. Can you build a nature pool yourself?

Yes, you can build a nature pool yourself, but the project involves more than excavating a hole and adding a liner. Structure, waterproofing, water flow and biological filtration must work together. You also need to plan safety, excavated soil disposal and access for future maintenance.

A natural pool drawing needs adapting to the site's levels, soil and groundwater. Bringing in an experienced professional for design and critical construction stages can reduce the risk of leaks, inadequate filtration and costly rework, while leaving room for work you want to do yourself. Our guide to building your own nature pool helps you decide which parts to take on.

4. How much maintenance does a nature pool need?

Routine nature pool maintenance mainly involves collecting leaves, emptying debris collectors and checking water level and circulation. Plants, bottom sediment and equipment also need attention according to the care plan. The workload depends partly on pool size, nearby trees and how heavily the pool is used.

Natural pool care changes through the year, with more leaves in autumn and separate tasks for spring startup and winter preparation. Our guide to nature pool care through the seasons gives an overview. A well-planned system, accessible equipment and a clear care plan help make those tasks a manageable routine.

5. What is a nature pool and how does filtration work?

A nature pool is a constructed swimming space with biological water treatment rather than routine chlorine dosing. Filtration usually combines mechanical debris collection with biological filters, where microorganisms contribute to water treatment. Plants can be part of the system, but its overall sizing and water flow determine how it works.

Nature pool, swimming pond and biological pool describe related designs, although appearance and filtration technology can differ. A chlorine-free pool still needs checks and care; clear water alone does not establish good bathing-water quality. Learn more about how natural pool filtration works.

6. Can you heat a nature pool?

Yes, a nature pool can be heated when its filtration and equipment are designed for it. Your preferred swimming temperature and season therefore belong in the initial plan. A heat pump may be an option, but its size needs to suit the water volume, heat losses and temperatures you want.

Natural pool heating costs depend on weather, wind, cover use and how long the heating runs. Slightly warmer summer water is a different task from extending the season through cold spring nights. Our guide to heating a nature pool explains the options and what to include in your estimate.

7. How much space does a small nature pool need?

A small nature pool can be designed for dipping and cooling off, but the bathing area is only part of the space required. Filtration, edges, water access and equipment access also need room. A useful natural pool plan therefore shows the whole installation, not just the water dimensions.

Start with how you want to use it: cooling off after a sauna, bathing together or swimming longer lengths. There is no single minimum garden size for every system, but a smaller garden need not rule out a pool for dipping. Our guide to how much space a nature pool needs explains what to allow for. Careful planning can make room for both a swim and the rest of garden life.

8. Do you need planning permission for a nature pool?

In Sweden, the pool itself usually does not require building permission, but ground changes and surrounding structures may need permission or notification. Malmö City's pool guidance covers examples including decks, pool houses and water and drainage connections. Check the conditions for your own property.

Ask your municipality about building permission, ground works and any shoreline protection before excavating. Accident prevention still needs planning when building permission is not required. Our guide to nature pool safety and permissions in Sweden helps you prepare the questions. For a project in Denmark, check Danish requirements with the local municipality.

9. Do nature pools attract mosquitoes?

A nature pool does not automatically mean more mosquitoes, but no pool can guarantee a mosquito-free garden. Mosquito larvae develop in water, and standing water can provide suitable habitats. The question concerns both the pool's design and other collections of water nearby.

Keep circulation working and ask the installer to assess stagnant areas if problems arise. Check buckets, plant saucers and other containers that collect rainwater too; emptying them forms part of the CDC's advice on controlling mosquitoes around the home. Do not add pesticides to swimming water without first checking their suitability for bathing and biological filtration.

10. What happens to a nature pool in winter?

A nature pool can normally retain water through winter, but its water level, pumps, filters and pipework must follow the installation's winter plan. Some components may keep running, while others need draining, indoor storage or frost protection. Do not empty the whole pool on your own initiative.

Prepare before frost arrives and keep the protection around the water effective after the swimming season ends. Winter swimming needs separate planning. Our seasonal nature pool care guide covers winter preparation and spring startup. Even when you are not swimming, the pool's stone edges and surrounding planting remain part of the garden to enjoy through the changing seasons.
translations.blog.naturpool-fran-forsta-samtal-till-b:
Describe the life you want around the water

Start with what the pool should bring to your day: a morning dip, time together or more room to swim. Tell us where the property is, what you want to keep in the garden and the budget you are considering. You do not need a finished drawing or a chosen package before getting in touch.

Faunapoolen's first phone consultation is free. We discuss your idea, the property and a useful next step. Choosing a package in the enquiry tells us what interests you; it is not an order or a site-specific quotation. If you are still choosing, the package page helps you compare the starting options.

Assess the site and the questions it raises

The site assessment turns a general idea into questions that can be answered: available space, levels, access, the surroundings and where treatment and equipment could go. Photographs and a rough plan help prepare the discussion. Our space guide explains what to include.

Site visits are charged, and the fee is credited against installation if you proceed. Confirm the amount and what the visit covers before booking. A visit and a full design proposal are not interchangeable promises, so make the expected output clear.

Identify matters needing further investigation, such as ground conditions or an authority decision. Our safety and permissions guide provides questions to take to the relevant authority. A design conversation does not replace a required approval.

Make the proposal specific enough to compare

After assessing the site, we develop the design and quotation. Review how the swimming area, treatment, entry points and surrounding garden work together. Ask what is included in the finished result and what is an option or your responsibility. An attractive picture is only one part of understanding the offer.

  • Which drawing and dimensions describe the agreed pool?
  • Who handles excavation, removed soil, electrical work and water supply?
  • What is included around the edges, and which disturbed garden areas are reinstated?
  • How are protection, equipment access and later care addressed?
  • Which assumptions still need confirmation before a construction date is agreed?

The Swedish Consumer Agency recommends recording scope, price, payment and timing in writing, together with how changes and additional work will be handled. Its guidance on hiring a contractor is useful when reviewing an agreement. Ask about anything that remains open before accepting the proposal.

Agree a schedule around the actual work

There is no reliable build-time promise for every natural pool. The size of the work is only one factor: site access, investigations, decisions, material availability and weather can affect the sequence. Separate the time needed for planning from the period when the garden is a construction site.

Discuss a proposed start, key stages and what must be settled beforehand. Agree how you will be told about a delay or a newly discovered condition, and how its effect on the design, price and timing will be assessed. A shared decision at that point is more useful than an unexplained change later.

Build the agreed design

Construction brings together groundworks, the pool structure and sealing, circulation and treatment, followed by the agreed surrounding finish. The exact method comes from the project design. This overview is a guide to commissioning the work, not a construction recipe for your ground conditions.

Before work begins, clarify access to the house, where materials will be stored and how the work area is separated from everyday garden use. Keep a clear contact for questions during the build. For an example of a completed setting, see our Gotland project; its appearance does not establish a timetable for another property.

Handover should make ownership understandable

We start the system and show you how to care for it. Use the handover to understand normal operation, the tasks you are expected to do and the instructions for the installed equipment. Ask how readiness for swimming is checked, what needs attention during the first period and who to contact if something changes.

Keep the agreed documents and care plan together. Our seasonal care guide helps organize the questions, while your own handover instructions govern the details.

Compare the packages, then tell us about the pool you have in mind. If you intend to build yourself, the separate self-build guide addresses that route.

Reviewed: 17 September 2026. The project agreement sets the actual scope, responsibilities and schedule.
translations.blog.naturpool-i-sodra-sverige.bodyHtml:
A nature pool that belongs in your garden

A morning dip before work, a swim with the children or an evening beside the water: start with the moments you want to make room for. A nature pool brings swimming and garden design together, with biological filtration planned as part of the installation. The shape, edges and planting should suit both the house and the way you use the space.

Faunapoolen designs and builds nature pools in southern Sweden, including Skåne, Halland, Blekinge and Småland. We also work throughout Sweden and in Denmark. You do not need a finished drawing to begin a conversation about a pool we can build for you.

Planning a nature pool in Skåne, Halland, Blekinge or Småland

Whether your garden is in Malmö, Lund, Helsingborg, Halmstad, Karlskrona or Växjö, the property matters more than the postcode. Two nearby gardens can call for different layouts, ground preparation and construction access. A regional search is a useful way to find a pool builder; the proposal still needs to start with your own site.

Show us the route from the house, places where you enjoy sitting and views you want to keep. Note slopes, trees, narrow gates and any areas where water collects after rain. For an exposed garden, include where you find shelter and sun; beside mature planting, consider how the pool and its equipment will be reached for care.

Allow space for more than swimming

The swimming area is only part of a natural pool. Filtration, equipment, edges and paths also need a place in the design. A compact pool with comfortable surroundings can offer more day-to-day enjoyment than a larger pool that leaves no room to sit or move around it.

Our guide to the space a nature pool needs helps you think about the whole installation. For a real example of our work, explore Brita’s pool on Gotland, with its natural stone edges and surrounding garden.

Budget for a complete installation

When comparing the cost of a nature pool in southern Sweden, look beyond the swimming area. Ask what is included in excavation, handling of excavated material, filtration, planting and the finished surround. Access and ground conditions can change the work required, so a starting price is a guide rather than a quotation for your property.

Compare our nature pool sizes and starting prices, then consider which scale fits your plans. We develop the design and quotation around the site, your priorities and the agreed scope, so you can decide with a clearer picture of the project.

From an idea to a pool built by Faunapoolen

Bring a few garden photographs, your location, an approximate budget and your preferred timing to the first conversation. We will discuss what you want from the pool and how to take the project forward. A site visit is agreed separately and charged, with the fee credited against installation if you proceed.

You can read more about our process from the first conversation to handover. The aim is a pool designed for your home, with the construction, surroundings and future care considered together.
translations.blog.naturpool-pris.bodyHtml:
A useful nature pool budget covers more than the water you swim in. It includes the system that cleans it, the work below ground and the edges that connect it to your garden. Start with our nature pool packages and current prices, then use this guide to understand what is included and what needs a separate allowance.

What is included in the price of a nature pool?

A nature pool quotation should make the whole installation understandable: design, excavation, liner, filtration, pumps, pipework, stone edges and planting. Check which work is covered by the starting price and which items depend on your site. Start-up, care instructions and any follow-up should be described too. Our package overview is the starting point; the quotation for your garden confirms the agreed work.

Commissioning an installation is different from buying a liner and pump for a project you build yourself. When comparing nature pool prices, compare the finished work and responsibilities as well as the equipment. A low material price does not tell you the cost of an installed pool.

Biological filtration needs its own space and a planned flow of water. It belongs in the initial design and budget, together with the swimming area. Our guide to nature pool filtration explains what that part of the installation does.

What changes the cost of installing a nature pool?

Ground conditions and access

A level garden with a clear route for machinery calls for different work from a steep site behind a narrow gate. Rock excavation, groundwater work and restricted access are assessed separately. Removal and disposal of surplus soil also need to be included in the quotation; a place to dig is not necessarily a place to leave everything that comes out.

Swimming area and the whole footprint

A larger pool needs more excavation, lining and a filtration system suited to its size and use. The swimming area is only part of the footprint: edges, filtration and access take space too. Before comparing prices per square metre, check whether the quoted area means swimming water or the entire installation.

Stone, planting and the surrounding garden

Compare the proposed stone edges and aquatic planting, and check whether the price also covers terraces, decks or landscaping beyond the pool. Think about the route from the house, where you will sit and how you will reach the equipment. These choices can change the total budget even when the swimming area stays the same.

Services, transport and heating

Check how the quotation accounts for electrical supply, water filling and transport, including any separate charges. If you want warmer swims or a longer season, discuss heating and a suitable cover as part of the design. Neither should be assumed to be included in a package starting price. Our guide to heating a nature pool covers those choices.

Does a small nature pool cost less?

A smaller swimming area can reduce materials and excavation, but a small nature pool still needs reliable filtration, circulation and careful installation. Its price does not fall in direct proportion to its area. Difficult access or ground conditions can also make a compact project more involved than its size suggests.

Begin with the way you want to use the water. A short dip after a sauna needs a different layout from swimming with the family. Our smallest starting package has a swimming area from 17.5 m². The full installation needs more room for filtration and edges, with paths and terraces considered as well. Read how much space a nature pool needs before measuring only the water.

How to compare nature pool quotations

Ask each supplier to describe the same finished project. A useful comparison makes the scope, exclusions and responsibilities visible. Check these points together:

  • The swimming area, depth and space for filtration.
  • Design, excavation and any assumptions about ground conditions.
  • Soil removal, transport, electrical supply and filling.
  • Liner, pumps, filtration, pipework and installation.
  • Stone edges, aquatic planting and any separate garden work.
  • Start-up, handover, care instructions and follow-up.
  • VAT, payment terms and how changes to the agreed work are priced.

For a Faunapoolen project, the quotation should make the agreed scope and site-specific costs clear before construction. Use the package overview to compare our starting scopes, then read how a Faunapoolen project develops to see what happens between an idea and handover.

What does a nature pool cost to run?

The construction price and annual running costs answer different questions. Biological filtration replaces routine chlorine dosing, but circulation still uses electricity and the pool still needs care. Water top-ups, optional heating, service visits and eventual repairs also belong in the ownership budget.

There is no single annual figure that fits every installation. Equipment, operating hours, the swimming season and how much care you do yourself all matter. Our nature pool running-cost guide shows how to calculate a budget, while the aftercare checklist explains the routine.

See what the investment can become

A price list helps establish the scale of the decision. A real garden shows how a pool can fit into everyday life. Explore Brita’s nature pool on Gotland for a completed Faunapoolen project, its setting and photographs. It is an example of our work, not a quotation or a promise that another property will cost the same.

When you have a sense of your budget, explore our nature pools and consider the space, swimming and garden you want. You do not need to choose a package yet. The aim is to find a scale that feels right and understand what your own site would add to the starting price.
translations.blog.naturpool-sakerhet-och-tillstand.bo:
Ask about the whole project

A natural-looking pool still needs a clear assessment of the work being proposed. Describe its intended use for swimming, its position, the surrounding structures and any changes to ground levels. A product name such as natural pool or swimming pond is not an approval category that settles these questions.

Contact the municipality responsible for the property before committing to excavation. Ask which parts need a permit, a notification or further information, and what decisions must be in place before work starts. Keep the reply with the drawing it refers to; an answer about one layout may not cover a later change.

Check ground levels and surrounding structures

Halmstad municipality's pool guidance illustrates why the entire project matters: decking, a roof, walls and ground changes can raise separate permission questions, and a connection to the public water system can require notification. This is a municipal example, not a decision for properties elsewhere.

Prepare an existing-and-proposed view of the site. Show the pool, distances to boundaries and buildings, current and proposed ground levels, the equipment position and any enclosure or roof. Ask whether local planning conditions or protection of the area affect the proposal. Avoid relying on a neighbour's older project as evidence that yours has the same conditions.

Plan child protection as part of the design

Boverket's current guidance for fixed swimming pools on plots requires drowning protection that younger children cannot pass. It defines younger children as under six and gives no exemption based on pool size or shallow water. Confirm how the rules apply to the proposed installation.

Discuss the practical solution while the edges and access are being designed. How is protection kept effective between swims? Who closes or restores it? Can it be operated comfortably in everyday use? Ask for the intended solution to be documented, including its maintenance. A leaf-collection net should never simply be assumed to be a safety cover.

Adult supervision remains part of using water with children. Keep entry and exit points understandable and arrange the surroundings so you can watch the swimming area. If you are uncertain whether a proposed protection system suits an irregular shape, resolve that with the designer and responsible authority before it becomes a construction detail.

Include electrical planning early

Elsäkerhetsverket's pool guidance emphasizes following equipment instructions, using suitable outdoor equipment and protecting the supply with a residual-current device. It also warns against placing electrical appliances where they could fall into the water. Treat electrical placement as a design requirement, not a last-minute extension lead.

For electrical installation work, use a company registered for the relevant work and verify it through Elsäkerhetsverket's contractor information and register. Agree who coordinates the electrical installation with the pool design. The designer and electrical contractor need the actual equipment specifications; a general pond-pump description is not enough.

Establish how water enters and leaves

Ask the local water provider about filling, current restrictions and any connection requirements. For example, Växjö asks owners using municipal water to contact the municipality before filling. Its advice also makes the owner responsible for avoiding harm from pool water to surrounding properties and nearby private water supplies.

Describe overflow, maintenance water and any proposed emptying route separately. Ask the municipality or water provider which destination is acceptable for the water from your particular system. Do not assume that a storm drain, a ditch or a neighbouring low point is suitable merely because the pool is not routinely chlorinated.

Check the property's environmental constraints

If the property is near existing water or protected nature, check the applicable protection before deciding where to build. Naturvårdsverket's shoreline-protection guidance explains that protected areas can restrict structures and changes affecting access or habitats. The municipality or county administrative board can help identify the questions for the location.

Keep a short project record: the current plan, authority replies and decisions, agreed safety design, electrical responsibilities and water arrangements. Record unresolved points before a construction start is agreed. This guide concerns Swedish projects and was checked against the linked sources on 17 September 2026; those authorities determine the requirements for your case.

Discuss your natural pool project with us and bring the questions into the site assessment. An enquiry is the start of planning, not a regulatory approval.
translations.blog.pool-conversions.bodyHtml:
Converting an existing pool to a nature pool may be possible, but changing the cleaning system is only part of the work. The structure, sealing, pipework and garden must suit the proposed design. A site assessment establishes what is worth keeping and whether conversion is a sensible starting point.

Start with the condition of the existing pool

Collect drawings and information about the pool's age, construction and previous repairs. Cracks, unexplained water loss or changes to the surrounding ground need investigating before a new finish conceals them. The existing pool shape can inform the design; it does not establish that the structure is suitable.

Allow space for cleaning and circulation

A biological cleaning system needs room and a planned route for the water. Its layout depends on the bathing area, intended use and chosen equipment. Consider access to pumps and collection points at the same time as the visible pool edge.

Read how nature-pool filtration works to see why debris collection, biological processes and circulation must be planned together.

Decide what can stay

A survey should separate usable elements from those requiring repair or replacement. Discuss the shell, waterproofing, pipes, electrical equipment, steps and surrounding paving individually. Retaining an element is useful only if it suits the new system and remains accessible for maintenance.

Agree the process before construction

The first conversation establishes your wishes and what is known about the pool. The next assessment must define the proposed solution, work scope and remaining uncertainties before a quotation or construction schedule can be meaningful. Ask who is responsible for each stage and how unexpected structural work would be handled.

Understand what drives the cost

Access for machinery, removal of old materials, structural repairs, new cleaning equipment and changes around the pool all affect the work. Reusing a shell does not automatically make conversion cheaper than a new installation.

Our nature-pool packages and starting prices describe new-build alternatives. They are useful for comparing options, but they are not conversion quotations.

Plan commissioning and ongoing care

A changed system needs a commissioning and care plan. Ask how operation and water quality will be checked, when bathing can begin and what you will need to monitor. The bathing start date should follow the agreed commissioning checks for the completed system.

If you are still choosing between pool types, the comparison of conventional and natural pools explains the different approaches.

Gather these details for the first conversation

  • Photos of the pool, equipment and surrounding access.
  • Dimensions, drawings and known construction materials.
  • Details of leaks, repairs and existing treatment equipment.
  • Your desired bathing area, garden changes and budget.

Tell us about your existing pool. Describe it in the enquiry notes so we can discuss whether further assessment is appropriate.
translations.blog.skotsel-av-naturpool-under-aret.bod:
Begin with the plan for your pool

Natural filtration does not remove the need for care. At handover, make sure you understand which checks you can do, which tasks need a specialist and what changes between swimming season and winter. Keep the component names, manuals and contact details together so that advice can be matched to the equipment actually installed.

A useful care plan names the task, what prompts it and how to recognize a problem. “Check regularly” is less helpful than knowing the normal water level and where to look for a reduced flow. Avoid borrowing a cleaning schedule from another pool merely because it looks similar. The filtration guide explains the parts of the system in more detail.

Spring: inspect before restarting

Walk around the pool after winter. Look at the edges, access points and visible equipment, and record anything that has moved, cracked or become difficult to reach. Check what was disconnected or stored before restarting. Follow the installed system's sequence rather than switching everything on to see what happens.

In its seasonal care overview, natural-pool manufacturer Biotop includes plant care, circulation restart and removal of bottom sediment among spring tasks. That is an example from its own systems, not a universal timetable or confirmation that your pool uses Biotop equipment.

Ask which checks must be completed before swimming resumes, and arrange any required inspection in advance. A calendar date or a clear-looking surface alone should not be your handover criterion. Keep observations and any agreed measurements in a short record that is useful if a question arises later.

Summer: learn what normal looks like

Notice the water level, visible flow and collection of surface debris during ordinary use. Check baskets or screens as specified for your installation, especially after windy weather. Aquascape™'s pond-system instructions explain that excessive debris in the collection net can restrict flow. Their detailed procedures concern that equipment; use your own manual for cleaning and isolation.

Record unusual water loss rather than continually topping up without investigation. Note when it began, recent weather and whether the circulation setting changed. Check local filling restrictions before adding water. If the appearance or smell changes unexpectedly, pause swimming and ask for an assessment instead of choosing a treatment from a photograph.

For algae questions, start with our algae and maintenance guide. Avoid adding products or changing filtration settings without confirming their suitability for your swimming system.

Autumn: prepare before the first frost

Give leaf collection more attention as nearby trees shed their leaves. Decide how leaves will be removed without making the water harder to supervise. A leaf net must not be mistaken for a child-safety cover; protection around the pool needs its own appropriate design.

Biotop's autumn service guidance combines surface and planted-area care with equipment preparation. Use that as a reminder to review the whole installation. Agree which of your tasks are seasonal, which depend on condition and who will perform them. Plant cutting should follow the actual planting plan rather than a blanket instruction to cut everything back.

Winter: follow the installed equipment

Do not assume that every pump runs throughout winter, or that every pump should be removed. Oase's winter guidance distinguishes frost-resistant equipment from components needing protection. A rating for one component does not establish a winter operating plan for the pool, its pipes and its controls.

Before cold weather, confirm the intended water level, equipment settings, required protection and response to a power cut. Ask what must still be checked when you are away. Winter operation does not itself mean the installation is suitable for winter swimming. Keep the safety arrangements effective when the pool is not in use.

Know when to ask for help

Contact the installer when flow does not return to normal after the checks you were shown, when water loss continues, or when equipment behaves unexpectedly. Describe the symptom, equipment model and recent changes. That gives a professional a better starting point than a request for a generic cleaning product.

Planning a new pool? Compare the packages and discuss the ownership tasks alongside the design. For an existing installation, describe the system and the help you need so we can confirm whether we can assist.

Sources checked: 17 September 2026. Manufacturer examples illustrate why care must match the system; they are not a specification of Faunapoolen package equipment.
translations.blog.small-features-for-small-spaces.bod:
In a small garden, choose the experience you want before choosing the water feature. A fountain brings visible movement close to a seat. A waterfall can lead the eye through planting. A small pond offers a still water surface and a place for aquatic plants. Each needs room beyond the water itself.

Do you want to see water, hear it or swim?

Mark where you spend time and where a water feature would be visible from indoors. Listen to the garden before adding another sound. The result depends on the flow, drop, surfaces and surroundings, so a photograph cannot tell you how a waterfall will sound beside your terrace.

If swimming is the real wish, establish that first. A decorative feature is not a small swimming pool. The garden-planning article helps you connect the feature to paths, seating and views.

A fountain beside a small seating area

A fountain can concentrate the visible water in one spot. Consider the reservoir beneath it, the pump's access point and where splashing may reach. Leave space to lift out equipment and clean the collection area, even if the visible feature is modest.

A waterfall with a hidden reservoir

A pondless waterfall returns water to a reservoir hidden beneath the surface instead of a visible open pond at the bottom. The stream route, reservoir and access to the pump still require planning. Discuss the full footprint rather than only the width of the falling water.

Check how leaves can be removed and how water level is monitored. The absence of an open pond does not remove the need for supervision and an assessment of access around the feature.

A small planted pond, with or without fish

A pond can be planned around plants and the view of its water surface. Fish introduce further requirements for water volume, depth, oxygen, filtration and ongoing care. A small diameter alone cannot establish that a pond is suitable for koi. Decide whether fish belong in the plan before settling its size and equipment.

Leave room for installation and care

  • Measure access for materials and future equipment replacement.
  • Plan an appropriate electrical supply with the installer.
  • Make topping up, cleaning and pump access practical.
  • Discuss overflow, nearby surfaces and seasonal shutdown or operation.
  • Keep the route through the garden usable after the feature is installed.

A sketch showing those details makes it easier to choose between options. Explore our garden water features to start with the kind of water you want.

If you would rather take a dip

For bathing, read how much space a nature pool needs. Cleaning, edges and access come in addition to the swimming area. Our pool options and starting prices give a separate starting point for that conversation.
translations.blog.sports-stars-natural-ponds.bodyHtml:
A nature pool can be planned around your wish to take a short dip and spend time beside the water. If you also want to bathe during colder months, discuss that from the start: the design and operating plan must support the intended use. A summer pool is not automatically ready for winter bathing.

Decide how you want to use the place

Picture an ordinary visit: changing indoors, walking to the water, entering, getting out and returning to warmth. A short dip asks different things of the layout than swimming lengths or gathering with family. Explain your priorities before choosing a size.

Sports personalities and spectacular pool photos can inspire a project, but they do not demonstrate health or recovery benefits. Our focus here is the place, its everyday use and the questions needed for a workable design.

Plan the route between house, sauna and water

The shortest route on a drawing may cross a lawn that becomes wet or a step that is difficult to see. Consider the walking surface, changes in level, a place for towels and how the entrance is lit. If you have a sauna, include its position in the conversation. Sauna construction is a separate scope to agree, not an assumed part of a pool package.

Establish the limits of winter operation

Ask how pumps, pipes and water movement are managed in cold conditions and which parts of the system need winter preparation. Desired bathing use must be reconciled with the equipment instructions and the site's conditions. Do not assume the water will remain ice-free.

The guide to nature-pool care through the year helps you frame the seasonal questions. The operating plan for your installation should give the actual instructions.

Make access part of the design

Discuss entry and exit, handholds where needed, visibility after dark and how access to the water is controlled. Review how those details will work when surfaces are wet or icy. The guide to safety and planning questions gives a starting point for the wider assessment.

This is a guide to planning a bathing place, not an assessment of whether cold-water swimming is suitable for an individual. Pool design does not remove the risks associated with cold water.

Look at documented projects for relevant inspiration

Our completed nature pool on southern Gotland shows how a bathing place can become part of a garden. Use it for ideas about the setting and edges. The images and owner story do not establish winter operating conditions for another site.

A small bathing area or room for longer strokes?

A compact pool may suit the wish for a dip; swimming and shared use may call for more room. The swimming area is only part of the total space, which also includes cleaning, edges and access. Compare bathing areas and starting prices, then tell us how you hope to use the water.
translations.blog.vad-kostar-det-att-aga-en-naturpool:
Separate construction from ongoing costs

Use the price and package page for the advertised starting investment and scope. The budget here concerns what happens after construction. There is no single annual operating cost that reliably describes every natural pool: equipment, operating plan, optional features and how much work you do yourself all matter.

Ask for an ownership estimate alongside the proposal, with its assumptions written down. Keep electricity, water, care products, paid service and future repairs as separate lines. That makes it easier to see whether a low total leaves something out, and to replace an estimate with measured information after the first season.

Calculate electricity from input power and time

The Swedish Energy Agency explains the calculation: power in watts multiplied by operating hours gives watt-hours; divide by 1,000 for kilowatt-hours. For a cost estimate, multiply those kilowatt-hours by the relevant electricity cost per kilowatt-hour.

Use electrical input power, not a pump's water flow or a heater's heat output. A manufacturer's figure must correspond to the actual model and operating setting. For variable equipment, measurements over representative use are more helpful than assuming that the maximum rating applies all day. Ask the installer how consumption can be measured safely; do not introduce an unsuitable meter or extension lead around water.

A worked example with hypothetical assumptions
